newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan oil chief says deregulation to hurt profits.
newsitem.headline: Japan oil chief says deregulation to hurt profits.

text.p: The damage inflicted on Japanese oil firms' profits through deregulation will be serious, although the reforms themselves went more smoothly than expected, the nation's oil industry body said on Wednesday.
"Some oil firms are likely to see steep falls in profits (for the year ending March 31), in spite of an increase in sales," Petroleum Association of Japan (PAJ) chairman Yuji Idemitsu told reporters.
Japan's oil industry has been through a tough year since the liberalisation of oil product imports last April, but the impact was not as severe as initially anticipated, he said.
"We had expected a greater number of firms to start importing oil products after deregulation and were worried about competition," Idemitsu said.
Regulations restricting imports of oil products, such as gasoline and kerosene, to refiners were lifted last spring.
Now, in theory any company can import petroleum products.
Based on data up until December 1996, oil product imports by newcomers accounted for only seven percent of total imports or about five percent of total domestic demand, Idemitsu said.

He said interest in the import business waned last year, probably because profitability was squeezed due to a weaker trend in the yen against the dollar at a time when overseas oil product prices surged.

Idemitsu said oil companies had not been able to immediately pass on to the wholesale price the surging cost of procuring crude, caused by higher global market prices and a weaker yen against the dollar.
In order to combat imports after deregulation, oil firms devised a new wholesale pricing system which brought product prices into line with international market levels.
For the year ending December 1996, Mobil Sekiyu KK reported its current profits fell by 10.2 pct compared to a year earlier, while Showa Shell Sekiyu KK current profits were down 36.2 pct.
Other leading Japanese oil companies follow an April-March business year.
In February, Mitsubishi Oil Corp revised its parent current forecast for the year to March 31 to a loss of 9.50 billion yen from an earlier forecast of an eight billion yen profit.
